children: Bitcoin slid to $62,000 on November 15, its lowest level since July. The drop erased approximately 29% from the high of around $87,000 set on September 21.

The more revealing number sits underneath the price chart. Realized losses, the dollar value of coins sold for less than their owners paid, climbed to levels Glassnode says haven't appeared since the cycle lows of 2018, 2020, and early 2023.
Glassnode characterized the selloff as capitulation. That's the market's version of tapping out: holders selling at a loss because locking in the pain feels better than waiting for more of it.
The heaviest selling came from short-term holders. These are wallets that bought relatively recently and tend to react fastest when price turns against them.
The twist is that many in this group had already taken profits during the September-October rally. They cashed out near the top, then apparently bought back in time to sell near the bottom.

Realized losses are useful because they measure behavior rather than mood. A price chart shows where the market trades. Realized losses show who actually hit the sell button, and at what cost. Right now, that cost is historically high.
The damage extended well beyond spot holders. More than $2 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated within a 24-hour window, with long positions absorbing most of the hit.
Demand from the institutional side has been heading the other direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of more than $1.9 billion in the week ending November 13.
Widen the lens to the prior ten trading days and the total reaches $2.6 billion.
Stablecoins are sending a similar signal. Total stablecoin supply shrank 4.2% over a 90-day period, pointing to subdued demand across the crypto market.

At the lows, Bitcoin's market capitalization fell to approximately $1.3 trillion. The slide also extended a streak of six consecutive weekly declines, driven by the combination of ETF outflows and leveraged positions unwinding.
Realized loss spikes of this size have a history. The comparable readings in 2018, 2020, and early 2023 all arrived near what later proved to be cycle lows.
The reasoning is fairly intuitive. Once the most anxious holders have sold, fewer people remain who are willing to sell at a loss.
The $62,000 to $66,000 band is now the zone that matters most. Approximately 66,000 BTC were acquired within that range, meaning a large group of recent buyers holds a cost basis sitting right there.

If the range fails, the next reference point is the realized price of approximately $53,700. Realized price is the average cost basis of every Bitcoin, calculated from the price at which each coin last moved. A decisive break below $62,000 could trigger accelerated selling and another wave of liquidations.

Recovery attempts so far have been tepid. The capitulation data argues the worst of the forced selling may already be in the rearview mirror, while ETF flows and stablecoin supply suggest the buyers needed to replace it haven't arrived.

title: Bitcoin crashes to $62K as realized losses hit cycle lows
